source: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana Ch. 1 (Ayushkamiya Adhyaya), Verse 44
title: The Fundamental Principle of Opposites: Samanya-Vishesha Siddhanta
content: Charaka establishes the master axiom of Ayurvedic therapeutics: 'Sarvada Sarva-Bhavanam Samanyam Vriddhi-Karanam, Hrasa-Hetus Cha Visheshasya' — similarity in attributes (Samanya) is always the cause of increase, whereas dissimilarity / opposite attributes (Vishesha) is the cause of decrease and balancing. If Vata is dry and cold, consuming dry and cold items will further increase Vata (disease); introducing opposite qualities — warmth (Ushna), unctuousness (Snigdha), and grounding heaviness (Guru) — immediately restores equilibrium. This law governs all personalized dietary synthesis in AYUSHYA.
contraindications: Applying similar qualities to an already aggravated dosha creates rapid acute disease (Prakopa).

source: Charaka Samhita, Vimanasthana Ch. 6, Verse 12 & Madhava Nidana
title: The Four Functional States of Agni (Digestive Fire)
content: Jatharagni (digestive metabolic fire) manifests in four distinct states based on doshic influence: 1) Samagni (Balanced Fire): Normal healthy digestion; completely digests food eaten at proper times without gas or acidity. 2) Vishamagni (Erratic Fire - Vata Dominant): Sometimes digests rapidly, other times fails to digest small meals; causes bloating, alternating constipation, and dry stools. 3) Tikshnagni (Intense Hyper-Fire - Pitta Dominant): Consumes food excessively fast; causes thirst, hot flashes, heartburn, and ravenous hunger. 4) Mandagni (Sluggish Hypo-Fire - Kapha Dominant): Extremely slow digestion; even tiny meals cause heaviness, coated white tongue, lethargy, and excess mucus.
contraindications: Feeding heavy foods during Mandagni or severe fasting during Tikshnagni creates severe pathological damage.

title: Ama (Metabolic Endotoxins) Formation, Signs & Symptoms
content: When Jatharagni is impaired, the ingested food undergoes incomplete fermentation rather than clean digestion, yielding a foul, heavy, sticky metabolic residue called Ama. Ama clogs the micro-channels (Srotas), adheres to biological tissues, and serves as the root etiology of chronic disease. Classical clinical signs of Ama: thick white coating on the tongue, bad breath, chronic morning lethargy and heaviness (Gaurava), loss of appetite (Aruchi), unrefreshed waking, constipation with sticky foul-smelling stools that sink in water, and generalized joint aches without structural injury.
contraindications: Never administer tonifying rejuvenating herbs (Rasayanas) like Ashwagandha or Chyawanprash while acute Ama is present; herbs must be preceded by Ama-cleansing.

source: Sharngadhara Samhita, Purva Khanda Ch. 4, Verse 1-4
title: Kindling Digestive Fire vs Digesting Toxins (Deepana vs Pachana)
content: Sharngadhara establishes the clinical difference between two digestive therapies: 1) Deepana: Herbs and spices that rekindle sluggish digestive fire without directly digesting metabolic Ama (e.g., Cumin / Jeera, Fennel / Saunf). 2) Pachana: Herbs that directly digest and break down toxic Ama residues without necessarily increasing the digestive heat (e.g., Nagarmotha / Cyperus rotundus). 3) Deepana-Pachana Combined: Agents that both kindle the fire and digest Ama simultaneously (e.g., Dry Ginger / Shunthi, Black Pepper / Maricha, Pippali). Taking warm ginger water before meals provides dual Deepana-Pachana action.
contraindications: Contraindicated in severe internal hemorrhages, acute dehydration, and burning gastric erosions.
